column1: # Hadith 2 — Jibrīl: Islam, faith (īmān) and excellence (iḥsān) (Ibn Rajab's commentary, batch 1)

column2: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) said: While we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ one day, there appeared before us a man whose clothes were exceedingly white and whose hair was exceedingly black.

No trace of travel could be seen on him, and none of us knew him. He came and sat down by the Prophet ﷺ, rested his knees against his knees, placed his palms on his thighs, and said: O Muḥammad, tell me about Islam.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer, give the zakāh, fast Ramaḍān, and make pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it.”
He said: You have spoken truly. ʿUmar said: We were amazed at him — he asks him and then confirms what he says!
He said: Then tell me about faith (īmān).
He said: “That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and that you believe in the divine decree, its good and its evil.” He said: You have spoken truly.
He said: Then tell me about excellence (iḥsān). He said: “That you worship Allah as though you see Him; for if you do not see Him, He surely sees you.”
He said: Then tell me about the Hour.
He said: “The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking.”
He said: Then tell me about its signs.
He said: “That the slave-woman gives birth to her mistress, and that you see the barefoot, naked, destitute shepherds of sheep competing in raising tall buildings.”
Then he went away, and I stayed a long while. Then he said to me: “ʿUmar, do you know who the questioner was?”
I said: Allah and His Messenger know best.
He said: “That was Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you your religion.” Reported by Muslim.
Muslim, and not al-Bukhārī, recorded this hadith. He recorded it by way of Kahmas, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Buraydah, from Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar,
who said: The first to speak about the divine decree in al-Baṣrah was Maʿbad al-Juhanī. Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ḥimyarī and I set off for Ḥajj or ʿUmrah,

and we said: If only we could meet one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and ask him about what these people say concerning the decree. We happened upon ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb as he was entering the mosque, and my companion and I flanked him, one of us on his right and the other on his left.
I thought my companion would leave the talking to me, so I said: Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, there have appeared in our parts people who recite the Qurʾān and seek out knowledge —
and he described their ways — and they claim that there is no decree and that everything begins anew. He said: When you meet those people, tell them that I am quit of them and they are quit of me.
By the One by whom ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar swears, if one of them had gold the size of Uḥud and spent it, Allah would not accept it from him until he believed in the decree.
Then he said: My father, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, told me: While we were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ… and he mentioned the hadith in full.
He then recorded it through other routes, some going back to ʿAbdullāh ibn Buraydah and some to Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, and mentioned that some of their wordings add and some omit.
Ibn Ḥibbān recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ by way of Sulaymān al-Taymī, from Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar. Muslim recorded it through this route too, but did not give its wording.

It contains additions. Among them, concerning Islam, he said: “and that you perform Ḥajj and ʿUmrah, bathe after major impurity, complete the wuḍūʾ and fast Ramaḍān.” He said: If I do that, am I a Muslim? He said: “Yes.”
Concerning faith he said: “and that you believe in Paradise, the Fire and the Scale,” and here too he said: If I do that, am I a believer? He said: “Yes.”

At its end he said: “This is Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you the matter of your religion; take it from him. By the One in whose hand is my soul, I was never in doubt about him whenever he came to me before this time, and I did not recognise him until he had turned away.”
The two of them recorded it in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, who said: One day the Prophet ﷺ was out among the people when a man came to him and said: What is faith?
He said: “Faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His Book, the meeting with Him and His messengers, and that you believe in the final Resurrection.”
He said: O Messenger of Allah, what is Islam?
He said: “Islam is that you worship Allah without associating anything with Him, establish the prescribed prayer, pay the obligatory zakāh and fast Ramaḍān.”
He said: O Messenger of Allah, what is excellence?
He said: “That you worship Allah as though you see Him; for even if you do not see Him, He sees you.”
He said: O Messenger of Allah, when is the Hour?
He said: “The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking, but I will tell you about its portents. When the slave-woman gives birth to her mistress, that is one of its portents;

when you see the naked and barefoot become the heads of the people, that is one of its portents; and when the herders of young livestock compete in raising buildings, that is one of its portents. [It is] among five things that no one knows but Allah.”

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: “Indeed, with Allah alone is knowledge of the Hour; He sends down the rain and knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware” [Luqmān 31:34].

He said: Then the man turned away, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Bring the man back to me.” They went to bring him back but saw nothing, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “This was Jibrīl, who came to teach you the matter of your religion.”

Muslim recorded it in a fuller form than this. In it, among the traits of faith, is: “and that you believe in the decree, all of it”; and concerning excellence he said: “That you fear Allah as though you see Him.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded it in his Musnad from the hadith of Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
and also from the hadith of Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Ibn ʿĀmir, or Abū ʿĀmir, or Abū Mālik, from the Prophet ﷺ. In his hadith he said:
We could hear the Prophet’s replies ﷺ, but could not see the one speaking to him or hear his words. This is contradicted by the hadith of ʿUmar that Muslim recorded, which is more authentic.
The hadith has also been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ from the hadith of Anas ibn Mālik, Jarīr ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Bajalī and others.

It is a very great hadith, encompassing an explanation of the whole religion. That is why the Prophet ﷺ said at its end, “This is Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you your religion,” after explaining the level of Islam, the level of faith and the level of excellence: he counted all of that as religion.
The narrations differ over whether Islam comes before faith or the reverse. In the hadith of ʿUmar that Muslim recorded, he began by asking about Islam; in al-Tirmidhī and elsewhere,
he began by asking about faith, as in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah; and some narrations of ʿUmar’s hadith have him asking about excellence between Islam and faith.
As for Islam, the Prophet ﷺ explained it in terms of the outward acts of the limbs, in word and deed. The first of these is the testimony that there is no god but Allah

and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, which is an act of the tongue; then establishing the prayer, paying the zakāh, fasting Ramaḍān, and pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it.
These divide into bodily acts, such as prayer and fasting; a financial act, namely paying the zakāh; and acts composed of both, such as the Ḥajj for someone far from Makkah.

In Ibn Ḥibbān’s narration he added to these ʿUmrah, bathing after major impurity and completing the wuḍūʾ. This draws attention to the fact that all the outward obligations are included in what the name “Islam” covers.

Here we have mentioned only the fundamental acts of Islam on which it is built; an explanation of them will come in its place, in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, “Islam is built on five,” if Allah the Exalted wills.
His words in some narrations, “If I do that, am I a Muslim?”

and the reply, “Yes,” show that whoever fully carries out the five pillars of Islam becomes a Muslim in truth, although whoever affirms the two testimonies becomes a Muslim in legal status; once he has entered Islam through them, he is obliged to carry out the remaining traits of Islam.

Whoever abandons the two testimonies leaves Islam. Whether abandoning the prayer takes one out of Islam is a well-known matter of disagreement among scholars, and so is abandoning the rest of the five pillars of Islam, as we will mention in its place, if Allah the Exalted wills.
Among the evidence that all outward deeds are included in what the name “Islam” covers is the Prophet’s saying ﷺ: “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr: A man asked the Prophet ﷺ: Which [part of] Islam is best?
He said: “That you feed people and give the greeting of peace to those you know and those you do not know.”

In the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Ḥākim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Islam has signposts and markers like the markers of a road. Among them are that you worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, establish the prayer, pay the zakāh,

fast Ramaḍān, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, greet the children of Ādam when you meet them, and greet the people of your house when you go in to them. Whoever falls short in any of these has left a share of Islam, and whoever abandons them has cast Islam behind his back.”

Ibn Mardawayh recorded, from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Islam has a light and signs like the markers of a road. Their head and sum are the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger, establishing the prayer, paying the zakāh,

completing the wuḍūʾ, judging by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ, obeying those in authority, greeting one another, greeting your families when you enter your houses, and greeting the children of Ādam when you meet them.” There is weakness in its chain, and it may be mawqūf (stopping short of the Prophet ﷺ).
It is authentically reported, from the hadith of Abū Isḥāq, from Ṣilah ibn Zufar, from Ḥudhayfah, who said: Islam has eight shares. Islam is a share, prayer is a share, zakāh is a share,
jihād is a share, pilgrimage to the House is a share, the fast of Ramaḍān is a share, enjoining what is right is a share and forbidding what is wrong is a share; and whoever has no share has failed.
Al-Bazzār recorded it as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ), but the mawqūf version is more authentic.
Some reported it from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Ḥārith, from ʿAlī, from the Prophet ﷺ; Abū Yaʿlā al-Mawṣilī and others recorded it. The mawqūf version, stopping at Ḥudhayfah, is more authentic;
so said al-Dāraquṭnī and others.
His words “Islam is a share” mean the two testimonies,
because they are the emblem of Islam, and by them a person becomes a Muslim.

Leaving forbidden things is likewise included in what the name “Islam” covers, as it is reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Part of the excellence of a person’s Islam is his leaving what does not concern him.” This will come in its place, if Allah the Exalted wills.

This is also shown by what Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī recorded from the hadith of al-ʿIrbāḍ ibn Sāriyah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has struck a parable: a straight path, with two walls on either side of the path, in which are open doors, and over the doors hang curtains.

At the gate of the path is a caller saying: O people, enter the path, all of you, and do not turn aside. And a caller calls from within the path: whenever someone wants to open any of those doors, he says: Woe to you, do not open it, for if you open it you will go through it. The path is Islam;
the two walls are the limits of Allah;
the open doors are the things Allah has forbidden; the caller at the head of the path is the Book of Allah;
and the caller from above is Allah’s admonisher in the heart of every Muslim.”
Al-Tirmidhī added: “Allah invites to the Abode of Peace, and guides whom He wills to a straight path” [Yūnus 10:25].

This parable that the Prophet ﷺ struck shows that Islam is the straight path on which Allah the Exalted has commanded us to keep steadfast and whose limits He has forbidden us to overstep, and that whoever commits any forbidden thing has overstepped its limits.

As for faith, the Prophet ﷺ explained it in this hadith in terms of inward beliefs, saying: “That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the resurrection after death, and that you believe in the decree, its good and its evil.”

Allah has mentioned faith in these five fundamentals in several places in His Book, as in His words, Exalted is He: “The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. Each believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers: We make no distinction between any of His messengers” [al-Baqarah 2:285].

The Exalted also says: “Rather, righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets” [al-Baqarah 2:177]; and the Exalted says: “who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them; and who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and are certain of the Hereafter” [al-Baqarah 2:3–4].

Faith in the messengers entails faith in everything they told of: the angels, the prophets, the Book, the Resurrection, the decree, and all the other details they told of concerning the attributes of Allah the Exalted and the features of the Last Day, such as the Scale, the Bridge, Paradise and the Fire.

Faith in the decree, its good and its evil, has been included in these verses; and it was because of this phrase that Ibn ʿUmar narrated this hadith, using it as proof against those who denied the decree and claimed that everything begins anew —

meaning that it starts afresh without any prior decree from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Ibn ʿUmar was severe with them, declared himself quit of them, and stated that their deeds would not be accepted from them without faith in the decree.
Faith in the decree has two levels.

The first is believing that Allah the Exalted knew beforehand the good and evil, obedience and disobedience that His servants would do, before He created them and brought them into being, and which of them would be among the people of Paradise

and which among the people of the Fire; that He prepared for them reward and punishment as recompense for their deeds before He created and formed them; that He wrote this down with Him and recorded it precisely; and that the deeds of His servants proceed according to what was already in His knowledge and His Writ.

The second level is that Allah the Exalted created all the acts of His servants — disbelief and faith, obedience and disobedience — and willed them from them. This level is affirmed by Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah

and denied by the Qadariyyah. The first level is affirmed by many of the Qadariyyah and denied by their extremists, such as Maʿbad al-Juhanī, whose doctrine Ibn ʿUmar was asked about, and such as ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd and others.

Many of the imams of the Salaf said: Debate the Qadariyyah with [Allah’s] knowledge: if they affirm it, they are defeated, and if they deny it, they have disbelieved. They meant that whoever denies the eternal, prior knowledge of the servants’ acts, and that Allah divided them before creating them into the wretched and the blessed

and wrote that down with Him in a preserved Book, has belied the Qurʾān and so disbelieves by it; and that if they affirm this but deny that Allah created His servants’ acts, willed them and wanted them from them with a cosmic, decreeing will, they are defeated,
because what they affirm is a proof against them in what they deny.
There is a well-known dispute among scholars over declaring these people disbelievers.
As for those who deny the eternal knowledge, al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad stated explicitly that they are disbelievers, and so did other imams of Islam.
If it is said: In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ distinguished between Islam and faith, and made all deeds part of Islam
and not of faith; yet the well-known position of the Salaf and the hadith scholars is that faith is word, deed and intention, and that all deeds are included in what the name “faith” covers.
Al-Shāfiʿī related the consensus of the Companions, the Successors and those after them whom he met on this.

The Salaf vehemently condemned those who excluded deeds from faith. Among those who condemned whoever said this, and declared it an innovated view, are Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Maymūn ibn Mihrān, Qatādah, Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Zuhrī, Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr and others.
Al-Thawrī said: It is an innovated opinion; we found people holding something else.
Al-Awzāʿī said: Those of the Salaf who have passed on did not distinguish between faith and action.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to the people of the garrison cities: To proceed: faith has obligations, laws, limits and practices; whoever completes them has completed faith, and whoever does not complete them has not completed faith. Al-Bukhārī mentioned it in his Ṣaḥīḥ.
The reply is: The matter is as he has said. That deeds are included in faith is shown by His words, Exalted is He:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and who rely upon their Lord; who establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them. It is they who are the believers in truth” [al-Anfāl 8:2–4].
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said to the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays: “I command you to do four things: to believe in Allah alone — and do you know what faith in Allah is?
It is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, establishing the prayer, paying the zakāh, fasting Ramaḍān, and giving a fifth of the spoils.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet ﷺ said: “Faith has seventy-odd,

or sixty-odd, branches. The best of them is saying ‘There is no god but Allah’, and the least of them is removing something harmful from the road; and modesty is a branch of faith.” This is Muslim’s wording.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer; the thief does not steal while he is a believer;

and the drinker does not drink wine while he is a believer.” Were it not that leaving these major sins is part of what the name “faith” covers, the name “faith” would not be denied to someone who commits any of them,
because a name is denied only when some of the pillars or obligations of what it names are absent.

As for how to reconcile these texts with the hadith of Jibrīl (peace be upon him) asking about Islam and faith — the Prophet ﷺ distinguishing between them and including deeds in what “Islam” covers but not in what “faith” covers —

it becomes clear once a principle is established: some names, when used alone and without qualification, cover many things; but when such a name is paired with another, it comes to denote some of those things, and the name paired with it denotes the rest.

This is like the words “poor” (faqīr) and “needy” (miskīn): when either is used alone, it includes everyone in need, but when one is paired with the other, one of the two words denotes some kinds of people in need and the other the rest. So it is with the names Islam and faith:

when either is used alone, the other is included in it, and on its own it denotes what the other denotes on its own; but when they are paired, one denotes part of what it denotes on its own, and the other denotes the rest.
A number of imams have stated this meaning explicitly.
Abū Bakr al-Ismāʿīlī said in his epistle to the people of al-Jabal: Many of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah said: Faith is word and deed,

and Islam is doing what a person has been obliged to do — that is, when each name is mentioned separately alongside the other. When it is said “the believers and the Muslims”, both being mentioned separately, one of them is meant to convey a sense the other is not; but when only one of the two names is mentioned, it includes and covers them all.
Al-Khaṭṭābī also mentioned this meaning in his book Maʿālim al-Sunan, and a number of scholars after him followed him in it.

Its correctness is shown by the fact that the Prophet ﷺ, when he mentioned faith on its own in the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, explained it in the same terms in which he explained Islam when it was paired with faith in the hadith of Jibrīl;

and in another hadith he explained Islam in the terms in which he explained faith, as in the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasah, who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, what is Islam?
He said: “That you surrender your heart to Allah, and that the Muslims are safe from your tongue and your hand.” He said: Then which [part of] Islam is best? He said: “Faith.”
He said: And what is faith?
He said: “That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the resurrection after death.” He said:
Then which [part of] faith is best? He said: “Emigration.”
He said: And what is emigration?
He said: “That you forsake evil.” He said: Then which emigration is best? He said: “Jihād.”
So the Prophet ﷺ made faith the best part of Islam, and included deeds in it.
This detailed explanation brings out what is truly correct on the question of Islam and faith: are they one thing, or are they different?
Ahl al-Sunnah and the hadith scholars differ over this and have written a number of works on it. Some claim that the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah hold that they are one and the same thing;

among them are Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr. This view has been reported from Sufyān al-Thawrī, in the narration of Ayyūb ibn Suwayd al-Ramlī from him, and Ayyūb has some weakness.

Others relate from Ahl al-Sunnah that the two are distinguished, such as Abū Bakr ibn al-Samʿānī and others. Distinguishing between them has been transmitted from many of the Salaf, among them Qatādah, Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir, al-Zuhrī,

Ḥammād ibn Zayd, Ibn Mahdī, Sharīk, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, Abū Khaythamah, Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn and others, though they differ among themselves on how the two are distinguished. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn used to say “Muslim” and were wary of saying “believer”.

The detailed explanation we have given removes the disagreement. One says: When Islam and faith are each mentioned alone, there is no difference between them; but when the two names are paired, there is a difference between them.

What is truly correct regarding the difference between them is that faith is the heart’s assent, affirmation and knowledge, while Islam is the servant’s surrender to Allah, his submission and yielding to Him, and this is by action. It is the religion, just as Allah the Exalted called Islam a religion in His Book;
and in the hadith of Jibrīl the Prophet ﷺ called Islam, faith and excellence religion. This too shows that when one of the two names is used alone, the other is included in it,
and that they are distinguished only where one name is paired with the other. In that case what is meant by faith is the category of the heart’s assent, and by Islam the category of action.
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Islam is public, and faith is in the heart.”
That is because deeds appear in public, while the assent in the heart does not appear.
When praying over the dead, the Prophet ﷺ used to say in his supplication: “O Allah, whomever of us You keep alive, keep him alive upon Islam; and whomever of us You take, take him upon faith,”
because acts of the limbs are only possible during life; at death nothing remains but the heart’s assent.

From this the meticulous scholars said: Every believer is a Muslim. For whoever has made faith real and firmly rooted in his heart carries out the deeds of Islam, as he ﷺ said: “Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh: if it is sound, the whole body is sound,

and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.” The heart is never truly filled with faith without the limbs being stirred to the deeds of Islam. But not every Muslim is a believer, for faith may be weak, so that the heart is not fully and truly filled with it even though the limbs carry out the deeds of Islam;

such a person is a Muslim but not a believer in the complete sense, as the Exalted says: “The Bedouins say: We believe. Say: You do not believe; rather say: We have submitted, for faith has not yet entered your hearts” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:14]. They were not outright hypocrites, on the sounder of the two interpretations, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and others;

rather, their faith was weak. This is shown by His words, Exalted is He: “But if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not diminish anything of your deeds” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:14] — meaning, He will not reduce anything of their reward — which shows that they had enough faith for their deeds to be accepted.
The same applies to the Prophet’s words ﷺ to Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, when Saʿd said to him: Why did you not give to So-and-so, when he is a believer?
The Prophet ﷺ said: “Or a Muslim” — indicating that he had not attained the station of faith and was only at the station of outward Islam. There is no doubt that whenever inward faith weakens,

a weakening of the outward acts of the limbs follows from it too. But the name “faith” is denied to whoever leaves any of its obligations, as in his saying ﷺ: “The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer.”

Ahl al-Sunnah have differed over whether such a person is called a believer with deficient faith, or whether it is said that he is not a believer but is a Muslim. There are two views, and they are two reported positions of Aḥmad.

As for the name “Islam”, it is not removed by the absence of some of its obligations or the violation of some of its prohibitions; it is removed only by doing something that negates it entirely. Nothing in the authentic Sunnah is known to deny Islam to someone who leaves any of its obligations,
in the way that faith is denied to someone who leaves any of its obligations — although the word “disbelief”, and likewise “hypocrisy”, has been applied to committing certain forbidden acts.

Scholars have differed over whether someone who commits major sins is called a disbeliever, with a lesser disbelief, or a hypocrite, with a lesser hypocrisy. I do not know of any of them permitting the name “Islam” to be denied him outright,
except that it is reported that Ibn Masʿūd said: Whoever abandons zakāh is no Muslim. Possibly he considered him a disbeliever on that account, outside Islam.

Likewise it is reported that ʿUmar said, of those who were able to perform the Ḥajj but did not, that they are not Muslims. Apparently he believed them to be disbelievers, which is why he wanted to impose the jizyah on them, saying: They have not yet entered Islam, so they are still People of the Book.

Since it is clear that the name “Islam” is removed only by the presence of something that negates it and takes one out of the religion altogether, the name “Islam”, when used without qualification or accompanied by praise, includes the whole of faith, assent and the rest, as has already been seen in the hadith of ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasah.

Al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn Mālik, that the Prophet ﷺ sent out a raiding party, and it made a raid on a people. One of them said: I am a Muslim. But a man of the raiding party killed him.

The account reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he spoke harshly about it. The man said: He only said it to protect himself from being killed. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has refused me permission to kill a believer,” three times.

Were it not that faith and assent to the five fundamentals are included in Islam used without qualification, someone who said “I am a Muslim” would not become a believer merely by saying it. Allah has also told us that the Queen of Sheba entered Islam with this word:
“She said: My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit, with Sulaymān, to Allah, Lord of the worlds” [al-Naml 27:44]; and He told us that Yūsuf (peace be upon him) prayed to die in Islam.
All of this shows that Islam used without qualification includes the assent that is included in faith.
In the Sunan of Ibn Mājah, from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: “ʿAdī, accept Islam and you will be safe.” I said: And what is Islam?

He said: “That you testify that there is no god but Allah, testify that I am the Messenger of Allah, and believe in all the decrees, their good and their evil, their sweet and their bitter.” This is an explicit text that faith in the decree is part of Islam.

Moreover, the two testimonies are among the traits of Islam without dispute, and what is meant is not uttering their words without assenting to them. So it is known that assenting to them is included in Islam.

A group of the Salaf, among them Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, explained the Islam mentioned in His words, Exalted is He, “Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam” [Āl ʿImrān 3:19], as tawḥīd and assent.
When faith is denied of someone while Islam is affirmed of him, as with the Bedouins whom Allah told us about, what is denied is that faith is firmly rooted in the heart;

what is affirmed of them is a share in the outward deeds of Islam, together with a measure of faith that makes their deeds valid, for without that measure of faith they would not be Muslims. Faith was denied of them only
because they had not tasted its realities and fell short in some of its obligations. This rests on the view that the assent residing in hearts varies in degree, which is the correct view

and the sounder of the two reported positions of Aḥmad. The faith of the truthful ones (ṣiddīqūn), to whose hearts the unseen is disclosed until it becomes as though witnessed, so that it admits no doubt or misgiving,

is not like the faith of others who have not reached this degree, so that doubt would enter them if doubts were raised. That is why the Prophet ﷺ made the rank of excellence that the servant worship his Lord as though he sees Him,
and this is not attained by believers in general. Hence one of them said: Abū Bakr did not surpass you by much fasting or prayer, but by something that settled in his breast.
Ibn ʿUmar was asked: Did the Companions laugh?
He said: Yes, and the faith in their hearts was like mountains.
How far this is from someone in whose heart faith weighs a mere speck or a barleycorn,
like those of the people of tawḥīd who are brought out of the Fire! It may rightly be said of such people that faith has not entered their hearts, because it is so weak in them.

These questions — I mean the questions of Islam, faith, disbelief and hypocrisy — are of the gravest importance, for Allah has attached to these names felicity and wretchedness, and deserving Paradise or the Fire. The disagreement over what they denote was the first disagreement to arise in this nation: the opposition of the Khawārij to the Companions,

when they put the sinners among the people of tawḥīd entirely outside Islam, placed them within the bounds of disbelief, treated them as disbelievers, and on that basis held the blood and wealth of Muslims to be lawful. After them came the opposition of the Muʿtazilah, with their doctrine of a station between the two stations, and then the opposition of the Murjiʾah, with their claim that the transgressor is a believer with complete faith.

Scholars past and present have written many works on these questions. Among the imams of the Salaf who wrote on faith are Imam Aḥmad, Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām, Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah and Muḥammad ibn Aslam al-Ṭūsī.

Works on it multiplied after them from every sect. Here we have set down points that bring together many of the fundamentals of these questions and of the disagreement over them, and that will suffice, if Allah wills.
Section

We have seen that deeds are included in what the name “Islam” covers, and in what the name “faith” covers too, and we have mentioned the outward acts of the limbs that are included in this. The inward acts are also included in what they cover.

Included among the deeds of Islam are devoting one’s religion sincerely to Allah, giving sincere counsel to Him and to His servants, and keeping one’s heart free, towards them, of deceit, envy, rancour and the kinds of harm that go with these.

Included in what the name “faith” covers are: hearts trembling at the mention of Allah and humbling themselves on hearing His remembrance and His Book, and faith increasing through that; true reliance on Allah; fearing Allah in secret and in public; being content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion

and with Muḥammad ﷺ as Messenger; choosing to have one’s life destroyed by the worst kinds of pain rather than disbelieve; sensing Allah’s nearness to the servant and keeping Him constantly in mind; putting love of Allah and His Messenger before love of anything else;

loving for the sake of Allah and hating for the sake of Allah, giving for Him and withholding for Him, and making all one’s movements and stillness for Him; giving oneself freely to acts of obedience, whether of wealth or of body; gladness and joy at doing good deeds, and distress and sorrow at doing evil ones;

the believers putting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ before themselves and their wealth; abundant modesty; good character; loving for one’s believing brothers what one loves for oneself; consoling the believers, especially one’s neighbours; supporting and aiding the believers; and grieving at what grieves them.
Let us mention some of the texts that have come on this.

As for what has come about its inclusion in the name “Islam”: in the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad and in al-Nasāʾī, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥaydah, who said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, I ask you by the One who sent you with the truth: what has He sent you with?
He said: “Islam.” I said: And what is Islam?

He said: “That you surrender your heart to Allah, turn your face towards Allah, pray the prescribed prayer and pay the obligatory zakāh.” In another version of his: I said: And what is the sign of Islam?

He said: “That you say: I have surrendered my face to Allah and given myself over wholly to Him; and that you establish the prayer and pay the zakāh. Every Muslim is inviolable to every other Muslim.”
In the Sunan, from Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim, the Prophet ﷺ said in his sermon at al-Khayf in Minā: “There are three things over which the heart of a Muslim harbours no rancour:

doing deeds sincerely for Allah, giving sincere counsel to those in authority, and holding fast to the community of the Muslims, for their supplication encompasses those beyond them.” He told us that these three traits rid the Muslim’s heart of rancour.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Mūsā, the Prophet ﷺ was asked: Which of the Muslims is best?
He said: “The one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, forsake him or look down on him.
It is evil enough for a person to look down on his Muslim brother. All of the Muslim is inviolable to the Muslim: his blood, his wealth and his honour.”

As for what has come about its inclusion in the name “faith”, there are His words: “The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and who rely upon their Lord; who establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them. It is they who are the believers in truth” [al-Anfāl 8:2–4];

His words: “Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves at the remembrance of Allah and at the truth that has come down, and that they should not be like those who were given the Book before, whose time grew long so that their hearts hardened?” [al-Ḥadīd 57:16];
His words: “And upon Allah let the believers rely”; His words: “And upon Allah rely, if you are believers” [al-Māʾidah 5:23]; and His words: “And fear Me, if you are believers” [Āl ʿImrān 3:175].
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“He has tasted the flavour of faith who is content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion and with Muḥammad as Messenger.”
Contentment with Allah’s lordship includes contentment with worshipping Him alone, without partner, and contentment with how He manages the servant’s affairs and what He chooses for him.
Contentment with Islam as religion requires choosing it over all other religions.

Contentment with Muḥammad as Messenger requires contentment with everything he brought from Allah, and accepting it with submission and an open heart, as the Exalted says: “But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, and then find in themselves no discomfort at what you have decided, and submit in full submission” [al-Nisāʾ 4:65].

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “There are three things which, whoever has them, finds through them the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anything besides them;
that he loves a person, loving him only for Allah; and that he hates to return to disbelief after Allah has saved him from it as he would hate to be thrown into the Fire.”
In one version: “finds through them the taste of faith”; and in some versions: “the taste and sweetness of faith.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “None of you believes until I am dearer to him than his child, his father and all people”; and in one version: “than his family, his wealth and all people.”
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from Abū Razīn al-ʿUqaylī, who said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, what is faith?

He said: “That you testify that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger; that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to you than anything besides them; that being burned in the Fire is dearer to you than associating anything with Allah;
and that you love someone who is not related to you, loving him only for Allah. If you are like that, love of faith has entered your heart as love of water enters the thirsty on a scorching day.”
I said: O Messenger of Allah, how can I know that I am a believer?
He said: “There is no servant of my nation — or of this nation — who does a good deed knowing that it is good and that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will repay him for it with good,
and who does an evil deed knowing that it is evil, and seeks Allah’s forgiveness for it, knowing that none forgives sins but Allah, without his being a believer.”
In the Musnad and elsewhere, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever is pleased by his good deed and grieved by his evil deed is a believer.”

In the Musnad of Baqī ibn Makhlad, from a man who heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Pure faith is that when you do wrong, or wrong someone — your slave, your slave-woman or anyone else — you fast or give charity, and when you do good, you rejoice.”
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from Abū Saʿīd, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The believers in this world are of three kinds: those who believe in Allah and His Messenger,

then have no doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the path of Allah; the one whom people trust with their wealth and their lives; and then the one who, coming within reach of something he covets, leaves it for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”
Also in it, from ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasah, who said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, what is Islam?
He said: “Good speech and feeding people.”
I said: What is faith?
He said: “Patience and magnanimity.”
I said: Which [part of] Islam is best?
He said: “[That of] one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.”
I said: Which [part of] faith is best?
He said: “Good character.”

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī explained patience and magnanimity, saying: It is patience in keeping away from what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden, and magnanimity in carrying out what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made obligatory.

In al-Tirmidhī and elsewhere, from ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her), the Prophet ﷺ said: “The most complete of the believers in faith are those best in character.” Abū Dāwūd and others recorded it from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).
Al-Bazzār recorded in his Musnad, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Ghāḍirī, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There are three things which, whoever does them, has tasted the flavour of faith:

one who worships Allah alone, [knowing] that there is no god but Allah, and gives the zakāh on his wealth every year, willingly…” and he mentioned the hadith. At its end: A man said: And what is a person’s purifying himself, O Messenger of Allah?
He said: “That he knows that Allah is with him wherever he is.”
Abū Dāwūd recorded the first part of the hadith without the end.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“The best faith is that you know that Allah is with you wherever you are.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Modesty is part of faith.”
Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of al-ʿIrbāḍ ibn Sāriyah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The believer is only like the camel with a tender nose: wherever it is led, it follows.”
Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: “The believers are but brothers, so set things right between your brothers” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:10].

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The likeness of the believers in their mutual love, mercy and sympathy is that of the body: when one part of it complains, the rest of the body joins it in fever and sleeplessness.”
In a version in Muslim: “The believers are like a single man.”
In another of his versions: “The Muslims are like a single man: if his eye hurts, all of him hurts, and if his head hurts, all of him hurts.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Mūsā, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The believer to the believer is like a building, each part strengthening the other,” and he interlaced his fingers.
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from Sahl ibn Saʿd, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“The believer, among the people of faith, has the place of the head in the body: the believer feels pain for the people of faith as the body feels pain for what afflicts the head.”

In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet ﷺ said: “The believer is the mirror of the believer. The believer is the brother of the believer: he protects him from ruin and guards him in his absence.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Abū Shurayḥ al-Kaʿbī, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“By Allah, he does not believe; by Allah, he does not believe; by Allah, he does not believe.” They said: Who is that, O Messenger of Allah?
He said: “The one whose neighbour is not safe from his harm.”
Al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“He is not a believer who eats his fill while his neighbour goes hungry.”

Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Muʿādh al-Juhanī, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever gives for Allah, withholds for Allah, loves for Allah and hates for Allah” — Imam Aḥmad added: “and marries for Allah” — “has completed his faith.”

In a version of Imam Aḥmad’s, he asked the Prophet ﷺ about the best faith, and he said: “That you love for Allah, hate for Allah and keep your tongue busy with the remembrance of Allah.” He said: And what else, O Messenger of Allah?
He said: “That you love for people what you love for yourself and dislike for them what you dislike for yourself.” In another of his versions: “and that you speak good or keep silent.”
This hadith shows that remembering Allah much is among the best of faith.
He also recorded, from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ (may Allah be pleased with him), that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say:
“The servant does not merit pure faith until he loves for Allah and hates for Allah. When he loves for Allah and hates for Allah, he has merited Allah’s friendship (walāyah).”

He also recorded, from the hadith of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The firmest handhold of faith is that you love for the sake of Allah and hate for the sake of Allah.”

Ibn ʿAbbās said: Love for the sake of Allah, hate for the sake of Allah, befriend for the sake of Allah and take as an enemy for the sake of Allah, for it is only by that that Allah’s friendship is attained;

and no servant will find the taste of faith, however much he prays and fasts, until he is like that. Most of people’s brotherhood has come to be over worldly matters, and that will avail those who share it nothing.
Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī and Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī recorded it.
Section
As for excellence (iḥsān), it is mentioned in the Qurʾān in a number of places: sometimes paired with faith, sometimes paired with Islam, and sometimes paired with taqwā or with action.

Paired with faith, as in His words, Exalted is He: “There is no blame on those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, so long as they are mindful of Allah, believe and do righteous deeds, then are mindful of Allah and believe, then are mindful of Allah and do good (aḥsanū); and Allah loves those who do good” [al-Māʾidah 5:93];
and as in His words, Exalted is He: “Indeed, as for those who believe and do righteous deeds, We do not let the reward of anyone who does good work go to waste” [al-Kahf 18:30].

Paired with Islam, as in His words, Exalted is He: “Rather, whoever submits his face to Allah while doing good will have his reward with his Lord” [al-Baqarah 2:112]; and His words, Exalted is He: “Whoever submits his face to Allah while doing good has grasped the firmest handhold” [Luqmān 31:22].

Paired with taqwā, as in His words, Exalted is He: “Indeed, Allah is with those who are mindful of Him and those who do good” [al-Naḥl 16:128]. It is sometimes mentioned on its own, as in His words, Exalted is He: “For those who do good is the best, and more” [Yūnus 10:26].

It is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim that the Prophet ﷺ explained the “more” as looking upon the Face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in Paradise. It is fitting that this should be made the reward of the people of excellence,

because excellence is that the believer worships his Lord in this world with presence of heart and vigilant awareness, as though he sees Him with his heart and looks at Him while he worships; so the reward for that is looking at Allah with his own eyes in the Hereafter.

The opposite of this is what Allah the Exalted tells us of the recompense of the disbelievers in the Hereafter: “Indeed, from their Lord, that Day, they will be screened off” [al-Muṭaffifīn 83:15]. He made that the recompense for their state in this world,

which is the rust piling up on their hearts until they were screened from knowing Him and being aware of Him in this world; so their recompense for that is to be screened from seeing Him in the Hereafter.
His words ﷺ in explaining excellence, “That you worship Allah as though you see Him…” and what follows, point to the servant’s worshipping Allah the Exalted in this manner,

which is calling His nearness to mind, and that he is before Him as though he sees Him. That brings about fear, dread, awe and veneration, as in the narration of Abū Hurayrah: “That you fear Allah as though you see Him.”
It also brings about wholeheartedness in worship and exerting every effort to make it excellent, thorough and complete.
The Prophet ﷺ gave this counsel to a number of his Companions, as Ibrāhīm al-Hajarī reported from Abū al-Aḥwaṣ,
from Abū Dharr, who said: My dear friend ﷺ counselled me to fear Allah as though I see Him, and if I do not see Him, He sees me.
It is reported that Ibn ʿUmar said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of part of my body and said:

“Worship Allah as though you see Him.” Al-Nasāʾī recorded it. It is also reported from the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam, both as marfūʿ and as mawqūf: “Be as though you see Allah; and if you do not see Him, He sees you.”
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Anas, that a man said: O Messenger of Allah, tell me something, and make it brief. He said: “Pray the prayer of one bidding farewell,
for if you do not see Him, He sees you.”

In the well-known hadith of Ḥārithah — which has been reported through several mursal routes and also with a connected chain, the mursal being more authentic — the Prophet ﷺ said to him: “How are you this morning, Ḥārithah?”
He said: This morning I am a true believer. He said: “Consider what you are saying, for every statement has a reality.” He said:

O Messenger of Allah, my soul has turned away from this world, so I keep my nights awake and my days thirsty; it is as though I see the Throne of my Lord in plain view, as though I see the people of Paradise visiting one another in it, and as though I see the people of the Fire howling to one another in it.
He said: “You have seen, so hold fast: [you are] a servant whose heart Allah has illuminated with faith.”
It is reported from the hadith of Abū Umāmah that the Prophet ﷺ counselled a man, saying to him: “Be shy before Allah as you would be shy before two righteous men of your clan who never leave you.”
It is also reported through another route as mursal.
It is reported from Muʿādh that the Prophet ﷺ counselled him when he sent him to Yemen, saying: “Be shy before Allah as you are shy before a man of standing in your family.”
The Prophet ﷺ was asked about uncovering one’s nakedness when alone, and he said: “Allah is more deserving that one be shy before Him.”
Abū al-Dardāʾ counselled a man, saying to him: Worship Allah as though you see Him.

ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr asked Ibn ʿUmar for his daughter’s hand while they were both circumambulating, and he gave him no answer. Later he met him and apologised to him, saying: We were in the circumambulation, picturing Allah before our eyes.
Abū Nuʿaym and others recorded it.
His words ﷺ: “for if you do not see Him, He surely sees you.”

It has been said that this gives the reason for the first part. When the servant is commanded to be vigilantly aware of Allah in worship and to call to mind His nearness to His servant until it is as though the servant sees Him, he may find that hard; so he seeks help in it from his faith that Allah sees him,

knows his secret and his open affairs, his inward and his outward, and that nothing of his affairs is hidden from Him. Once he has made this station real, it becomes easy for him to move on to the second station, which is gazing constantly, with the eye of insight, at Allah’s nearness to His servant and His being with him, until it is as though he sees Him.

It has also been said, on the contrary, that it indicates that whoever finds it hard to worship Allah as though he sees Him should worship Allah in the knowledge that Allah sees him and observes him, and so be shy of His gaze upon him; as one of those who know Allah said: Fear Allah, lest His gaze be the one you heed least of all who look at you.
Another said: Fear Allah in proportion to His power over you, and be shy before Allah in proportion to His nearness to you.
One of the women of the Salaf who knew Allah said: Whoever acts for Allah upon witnessing [Him] knows [Him]; and whoever acts upon Allah’s witnessing of him is sincere.
She was pointing to the two stations already mentioned.

The first is the station of sincerity: that the servant acts while calling to mind that Allah witnesses him, observes him and is near to him. When the servant calls this to mind in his deed and acts upon it, he is sincere towards Allah,
because calling this to mind in his deed keeps him from turning to anyone other than Allah or intending anyone else by his deed.

The second is the station of witnessing: that the servant acts in accordance with his witnessing of Allah the Exalted with his heart. This is when the heart is illuminated with faith and insight penetrates into knowledge of Allah, until the unseen becomes as though seen.
This is the reality of the station of excellence pointed to in the hadith of Jibrīl (peace be upon him), and the people of this station differ in it according to how deeply their insight penetrates.

A group of scholars explained in this sense the highest likeness mentioned in His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: “His is the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth” [al-Rūm 30:27]. Similar to it are His words, Exalted is He:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is as a niche in which is a lamp” [al-Nūr 24:35] — meaning the likeness of His light in the heart of the believer. So said Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and others of the Salaf.

We have already cited the hadith “The best faith is that you know that Allah is with you wherever you are,” and the hadith: What is a person’s purifying himself? He said: “That he knows that Allah is with him wherever he is.”

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Three will be in the shade of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, the Day when there is no shade but His: a man who, wherever he turns, knows that Allah is with him…” and he mentioned the hadith.

The Qurʾān indicates this meaning in a number of places, such as His words, Exalted is He: “When My servants ask you about Me, I am near: I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me” [al-Baqarah 2:186]; His words, Exalted is He: “He is with you wherever you are” [al-Ḥadīd 57:4];

His words: “There is no private conversation of three but He is their fourth, nor of five but He is their sixth, nor fewer than that nor more but He is with them wherever they are” [al-Mujādilah 58:7];

His words: “You are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite any of the Qurʾān, nor do you do any deed, but We are witnesses over you when you are absorbed in it” [Yūnus 10:61]; His words: “We are nearer to him than his jugular vein” [Qāf 50:16]; and His words: “They do not hide from Allah, while He is with them” [al-Nisāʾ 4:108].
Authentic hadiths have come urging that this nearness be called to mind during acts of worship, such as his saying ﷺ: “When one of you stands to pray, he is only conversing intimately with his Lord,

or his Lord is between him and the qiblah”; his saying: “Allah is before his face when he prays”; and his saying: “Allah sets His Face towards the face of His servant in his prayer as long as he does not turn away.”

And his saying to those who raised their voices in remembrance: “You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing and near.” In one version: “He is nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount”; and in another: “He is nearer to one of you than his jugular vein.”
And his saying: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: I am with My servant when he remembers Me and his lips move with My mention.”

And his saying: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: I am with My servant’s expectation of Me, and I am with him wherever he remembers Me. If he remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself; if he remembers Me in an assembly,

I remember him in an assembly better than it. If he draws near to Me by a hand’s span, I draw near to him by a cubit; if he draws near to Me by a cubit, I draw near to him by an arm’s span; and if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running.”
Whoever takes from any of these texts the likening of Allah to His creation, His indwelling in it or His union with it has been led there only by his ignorance
and his poor understanding of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ; Allah and His Messenger are free of all of that. Glory be to Him, of whom there is nothing like, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.

Bakr al-Muzanī said: Who is like you, son of Ādam? The way lies open for you to the prayer niche and the water: whenever you wish, you go in to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with no interpreter between you and Him.
Whoever comes to call this to mind while remembering and worshipping Allah will inevitably find intimacy with Allah and estrangement from His creation.
Thawr ibn Yazīd said: I read in one of the books that ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) said: O company of disciples, speak to Allah much and speak to people little. They said: How can we speak to Allah much?
He said: Be alone with Him in intimate converse; be alone with Him in supplication.
Abū Nuʿaym recorded it.

He also recorded, with his chain of narration, from Riyāḥ, who said: There was a man among us who prayed a thousand rakʿahs every day and night until he lost the use of his legs, and then he would pray a thousand rakʿahs sitting.

When he had prayed ʿaṣr, he would sit with his knees drawn up and wrapped, face the qiblah and say: I am amazed at creatures — how can they find intimacy with anyone but You? No, I am amazed at creatures — how can their hearts be lit by the remembrance of anyone but You?
Abū Usāmah said: I went in to see Muḥammad ibn al-Naḍr al-Ḥārithī and saw that he seemed withdrawn. I said: It seems you dislike being visited?
He said: Yes. I said: Do you not feel lonely?
He said: How can I feel lonely when He says: I am the companion of whoever remembers Me?
Mālik ibn Mighwal was asked, while sitting alone in his house: Do you not feel lonely?
He said: Does anyone feel lonely with Allah?

Ḥabīb Abū Muḥammad used to keep to himself in his house, saying: Whoever’s eye is not delighted by You, may his eye never be delighted; and whoever does not find intimacy with You, may he never find intimacy.
Ghazwān said: I have found rest for my heart in sitting with the One who holds what I need.
Muslim ibn Yasār said: Those who seek delight have found no delight like being alone in intimate converse with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Muslim the worshipper said: Were it not for the congregational prayer, I would never go out of my door until I died. He also said:

Those who obey Allah find no pleasure in this world sweeter than being alone in intimate converse with their Master, and I do not think that in the Hereafter, of all the immense reward, there will be anything greater in their breasts or more delightful to their hearts than looking at Him. Then he fainted.

Ibrāhīm ibn Adham said: The highest of degrees is that you devote yourself wholly to your Lord and find intimacy with Him with your heart, your mind and all your limbs, so that you hope in none but your Lord
and fear nothing but your sin, and His love is so firmly rooted in your heart that you prefer nothing to it. When you are like that, you will not care whether you are on land
or at sea, on the plain or on the mountain; your longing to meet the Beloved will be like the thirsty man’s longing for cold water
and the hungry man’s longing for good food; and the remembrance of Allah will be sweeter to you than honey, sweeter than pure fresh water to the thirsty on a summer’s day.
Al-Fuḍayl said: Blessed is he who feels estranged from people and has Allah as his companion.
Abū Sulaymān said: May Allah never let me find intimacy except with Him.
Maʿrūf said to a man: Rely on Allah until He is your companion, your intimate friend and the One to whom you bring your complaints.

Dhū al-Nūn said: Among the signs of those who love Allah is that they find intimacy with none but Him and feel no loneliness with Him. Then he said: When love of Allah the Exalted dwells in the heart, it finds intimacy with Allah,
because Allah is too majestic in the breasts of those who know Him for them to love anyone besides Him.
What the people of this path have said on this subject would take very long to relate, and what we have mentioned is sufficient, if Allah the Exalted wills.
Whoever reflects on what we have pointed to of what this great hadith indicates will know that all the sciences and branches of knowledge go back to this hadith and come under it,
and that the sciences discussed by all the scholars of the various groups of this nation do not go beyond this hadith and what it indicates, in summary and in detail.

The jurists discuss the acts of worship that are among the traits of Islam, adding to them discussion of the rulings on property, marriage and blood; and all of that belongs to the knowledge of Islam, as was pointed out earlier.

Yet much of the knowledge of Islam — its manners, its character and so on — remains, and only a few of them discuss it; nor do they discuss the meaning of the two testimonies, which are the foundation of all of Islam.
Those who discuss the fundamentals of religion discuss the two testimonies, faith in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and faith in the decree.

Those who discuss the knowledge of spiritual insight and of dealings with Allah discuss the station of excellence and the inward deeds that are also included in faith, such as fear, love, reliance, contentment, patience

and the like. So the sciences of the Sharīʿah that the groups of Muslims discuss are all contained in this hadith and all go back to it. This hadith alone is sufficient, and to Allah belong all praise and favour.
It remains to discuss what the hadith says about the Hour.

Jibrīl (peace be upon him) said, “Tell me about the Hour,” and the Prophet ﷺ said, “The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking,” meaning that all of creation are equal in their knowledge of when the Hour will come.

This indicates that Allah the Exalted has kept knowledge of it to Himself. That is why, in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said “among five things that no one knows but Allah the Exalted”, and then recited:

“Indeed, with Allah alone is knowledge of the Hour; He sends down the rain and knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware” [Luqmān 31:34].

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: “They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive? Say: Knowledge of it is only with my Lord; none but He will reveal it at its time. It weighs heavily on the heavens and the earth; it will come upon you only suddenly” [al-Aʿrāf 7:187].

In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The keys of the unseen are five, which no one knows but Allah.” Then he recited this verse: “Indeed, with Allah alone is knowledge of the Hour…” [Luqmān 31:34], to the end of the verse.

Imam Aḥmad recorded it, and his wording is that the Prophet ﷺ said: “I have been given the keys of everything except the five”: “Indeed, with Allah alone is knowledge of the Hour…” [Luqmān 31:34], to the end of the verse.

He also recorded, with his chain of narration, that Ibn Masʿūd said: Your Prophet ﷺ was given the keys of everything except five: “Indeed, with Allah alone is knowledge of the Hour…” [Luqmān 31:34], to the end of the verse.
His words: Then tell me about its signs —
that is, the marks that show it is near. In the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “I will tell you about its portents,” and these too are its signs.
The Prophet ﷺ mentioned two signs of the Hour.

The first: “that the slave-woman gives birth to her mistress”, her mistress meaning her lady and owner; in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah it is “her master”. This points to the conquest of lands and to slaves being brought in great numbers, until concubines become many

and have many children. The mother is then the slave of her master, and her children by him have his standing, for the master’s child has the standing of the master; so the slave-woman’s child comes to have the standing of her lord and master.

Al-Khaṭṭābī mentioned that this was cited as evidence by those who say that a slave-woman who has borne her master a child (umm walad) is freed in favour of her child out of his share of his father’s estate — that she passes to her children by inheritance and so becomes free on their account — and that she may be sold before her master’s death. He said: This inference is open to question.
I say: Some have cited it as evidence for the opposite: that the umm walad may not be sold, and that she is freed by her master’s death in every case,
because he made the slave-woman’s child her lord, as if it were her child who freed her, so that her freedom is attributed to him,
since he is its cause; so he became, as it were, her patron.
This is like what is reported of the Prophet ﷺ, that he said of his umm walad Māriyah when she gave birth to Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him): “Her child has freed her.”

Imam Aḥmad cited it as evidence, for he said, in the narration of Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥakam from him: “The slave-woman gives birth to her mistress” — mothers of children will become many. He meant: when she gives birth, she is freed on account of her child. He also said: In it is a proof that mothers of children may not be sold.

“The slave-woman gives birth to her mistress” has also been explained as meaning that slaves will be brought in such numbers that a daughter is brought and freed, then the mother is brought and the daughter buys her and puts her to work, not knowing that she is her mother; and this has happened in Islam.
It has also been said that it means slave-women will give birth to kings. Wakīʿ said: It means the non-Arabs will give birth to Arabs, and the Arabs are the kings and lords of the non-Arabs.
The second sign: “that you see the barefoot, naked, destitute (ʿālah)”.
By ʿālah are meant the poor, as in His words, Exalted is He: “and He found you poor (ʿāʾilan) and made you rich” [al-Ḍuḥā 93:8].
And his words: “shepherds of sheep competing in raising tall buildings.”

So it is in the hadith of ʿUmar. What is meant is that the lowest of people will become their leaders, and their wealth will grow until they vie with one another in the height of their buildings, their ornament and their fine workmanship.
In the hadith of Abū Hurayrah he mentioned three signs, among them that the barefoot and naked become the heads of the people, and that the herders of young livestock compete in raising buildings.
ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAṭāʾ narrated this hadith from ʿAbdullāh ibn Buraydah, and said in it:

“and that you see the deaf, the dumb, the blind, the barefoot, shepherds of sheep, competing in raising buildings — kings of the people.” He said: The man then rose and went away, and we said: O Messenger of Allah, who are these you have described?
He said: “They are the Bedouin Arabs (al-ʿurayb).”
ʿAlī ibn Zayd likewise narrated this last wording, from Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, from Ibn ʿUmar.
As for the earlier wordings, they are in the Ṣaḥīḥ, in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, with the same meaning.
His words “the deaf, the dumb, the blind” point to their ignorance and their lack of knowledge and understanding.

There are a number of hadiths with this meaning. Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Ḥudhayfah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Hour will not come until the happiest of people in this world is a base man son of a base man (lukaʿ ibn lukaʿ).”
In the Ṣaḥīḥ of Ibn Ḥibbān, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “This world will not come to an end until it is in the hands of a base man son of a base man.”
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Dharr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Hour will not come until a base man son of a base man prevails over this world.”

Imam Aḥmad and al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Before the Hour there will be years of deception, in which the trustworthy will be suspected, the suspect will be trusted, and the ruwaybiḍah will speak.”
They said: And what is the ruwaybiḍah?
He said: “The fool who speaks about the affairs of the public.”
In one version: “The transgressor who speaks about the affairs of the public.”

In Imam Aḥmad’s version: “Before the Dajjāl there will be years of deception, in which the liar will be believed and the truthful called a liar, the trustworthy thought treacherous and the treacherous trusted,” and he mentioned the rest.
The gist of the portents of the Hour mentioned in this hadith comes down to affairs being entrusted to those not fit for them, as the Prophet ﷺ said to someone who asked him about the Hour:

“When the matter is entrusted to those not fit for it, then wait for the Hour.” For when the barefoot, naked shepherds of sheep — people of ignorance and coarseness — become the heads of the people and the owners of riches and wealth, until they compete in raising buildings,

the order of religion and of the world is corrupted by it. When someone who was poor and destitute comes to lead people and becomes king over them, whether his rule is general or limited to certain matters, he will hardly give people their rights;

rather, he will keep for himself the wealth he has seized from them. One of the Salaf said: For you to put your hand into a dragon’s mouth and have it bitten off is better for you than to stretch it out to the hand of a rich man who has known poverty.
And if, besides this, he is ignorant and coarse, religion is corrupted by it,

because he has no concern for setting right people’s religion or teaching them; his concern is collecting wealth and hoarding it, and he does not care how much of people’s religion is corrupted, nor which of those in need are left to perish.
In another hadith: “The Hour will not come until the hypocrites of every tribe become its chiefs.”

When the kings and heads of the people are in this state, all other states are turned upside down: the liar is believed and the truthful called a liar, the treacherous trusted and the trustworthy thought treacherous; the ignorant speak and the scholar is silent, or is absent altogether, as it is authentically reported that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Among the portents of the Hour are that knowledge will be taken away and ignorance will prevail”; and he told us “that knowledge will be taken away by taking the scholars, until, when no scholar remains, people will take ignorant leaders, who will be asked and give rulings without knowledge, and so go astray and lead others astray.”
Al-Shaʿbī said: The Hour will not come until knowledge becomes ignorance and ignorance becomes knowledge.
All of this belongs to the overturning of realities and the reversal of affairs at the end of time.
In the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Ḥākim, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, as marfūʿ: “Among the portents of the Hour are that the best people will be brought low and the worst raised up.”

His words “competing in raising buildings” are evidence condemning vying and boasting, especially by competing in raising buildings. Tall building was not known in the time of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions;

rather, their buildings were low, as much as was needed. Abū al-Zinād reported from al-Aʿraj, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The Hour will not come until people compete in raising buildings.” Al-Bukhārī recorded it.
Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ went out and saw a lofty domed building, and said: “What is this?”
They said: This belongs to So-and-so, a man of the Anṣār. Its owner came and greeted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but he turned away from him. He did this several times, so the man demolished it.

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded it by another route, also from Anas, and in his version the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every building higher than this” — and he gestured with his hand like this, over his head — “is a burden on its owner.”

Ḥurayth ibn al-Sāʾib reported that al-Ḥasan said: I used to go into the houses of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ during the caliphate of ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him), and I could touch their ceilings with my hand.
It is reported that ʿUmar wrote: Do not build your buildings tall, for that will be the worst of your days.
Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād said: Ḥudhayfah said to Salmān: Shall we not build you a dwelling, Abū ʿAbdillāh?
He said: Why — to make me a king?

He said: No, but we will build you a house of reeds and roof it with reed mats; when you stand up it will almost touch your head, and when you lie down it will almost touch your head and your feet. He said: It is as though you had been inside my mind.
ʿAmmār ibn Abī ʿAmmār said: When a man raises his building higher than seven cubits, a voice calls out: O most wicked of the wicked, where are you going?
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded all of this.

Yaʿqūb ibn Shaybah said in his Musnad: It reached me from Ibn ʿĀʾishah: Ibn Abī Shumaylah told us: The Muslims settled around the mosque — meaning in al-Baṣrah — in tents of hair, and theft became widespread among them. They wrote to ʿUmar,

and he permitted them reeds, so they built with reeds; then fires became widespread among them. They wrote to ʿUmar, and he permitted them clay, but forbade anyone to raise his roof more than seven cubits, and said: When you build your houses with it, build the mosque with it too.

Ibn ʿĀʾishah said: ʿUtbah ibn Ghazwān had built the mosque of al-Baṣrah with reeds. He said: Whoever prayed in it when it was of reeds is better than whoever prayed in it when it was of mud brick, and whoever prayed in it when it was of mud brick is better than whoever prayed in it when it was of baked brick.
Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Hour will not come until people vie with one another in mosques.”
And, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “I see that after me you will raise your mosques high, as the Jews raised their synagogues high and the Christians their churches.”

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā reported, with his chain of narration, from Ismāʿīl ibn Muslim, from al-Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ built the mosque, he said: “Build it as a shelter like the shelter of Mūsā.”
Al-Ḥasan was asked: What was the shelter of Mūsā?
He said: When he raised his hand, it reached the shelter — meaning
the roof.
